claim: Porifera (sponges) are considered one of the oldest surviving phyletic lineages of animals, diverging from other metazoans around 700 Mya (Erwin et al., 2011).
source: Porifera (sponges) are considered one of the oldest surviving phyletic lineages of animals, diverging from other metazoans around 700 Mya (Erwin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Erwin et al., 2011, which provides the temporal estimate for sponge divergence.

claim: Sponges lack a gut, nerves and muscles.
source: Despite being one of the morphologically simplest animals, lacking a gut, nerves and muscles, sponges possess an extensive gene repertoire for transcriptional regulation required in eumetazoan development and body patterning (Srivastava et al., 2010; Larroux et al., 2008, 2006; Adamska et al., 2007; Gaiti et al., 2015; Nakanishi et al., 2014; Conaco et al., 2012; Riesgo et al., 2014; Grimson et al., 2008; Richards et al., 2008; Leininger et al., 2014; Fortunato et al., 2015, 2014; Bråte et al., 18212015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about sponge morphology.

claim: Sponges possess an extensive gene repertoire for transcriptional regulation required in eumetazoan development and body patterning.
source: Despite being one of the morphologically simplest animals, lacking a gut, nerves and muscles, sponges possess an extensive gene repertoire for transcriptional regulation required in eumetazoan development and body patterning (Srivastava et al., 2010; Larroux et al., 2008, 2006; Adamska et al., 2007; Gaiti et al., 2015; Nakanishi et al., 2014; Conaco et al., 2012; Riesgo et al., 2014; Grimson et al., 2008; Richards et al., 2008; Leininger et al., 2014; Fortunato et al., 2015, 2014; Bråte et al., 18212015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on sponge genomics.

claim: Amphimedon queenslandica has dynamic developmental gene expression akin to eumetazoans.
source: Here, following on from our recent transcriptomic studies that revealed that the sponge Amphimedon queenslandica (herein Amphimedon) has dynamic developmental gene expression akin to eumetazoans (Gaiti et al., 2015; Fernandez-Valverde et al., 2015; Levin et al., 2016), we set out to determine whether this transcriptional complexity is paralleled by regulatory complexity encoded by combinatorial histone PTM patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior transcriptomic studies.

claim: A complex gene regulatory landscape comprised of combinatorial histone modifications was already in place at the dawn of animals.
source: By analysing an extensive ChIP-seq compendium of histone H3 PTMs in this sponge, we show that a complex gene regulatory landscape comprised of combinatorial histone modifications was already in place at the dawn of animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Amphimedon enhancers are enriched in metazoan-specific microsyntenic units.
source: Strikingly, Amphimedon enhancers are enriched in metazoan-specific microsyntenic units, suggesting that their genomic location is extremely ancient and likely to place constraints on the evolution of surrounding genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on analysis of enhancer locations and microsynteny.

claim: The genomic location of Amphimedon enhancers is extremely ancient and likely to place constraints on the evolution of surrounding genes.
source: Strikingly, Amphimedon enhancers are enriched in metazoan-specific microsyntenic units, suggesting that their genomic location is extremely ancient and likely to place constraints on the evolution of surrounding genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of enhancers in microsyntenic units.

claim: The regulatory foundation for spatiotemporal gene expression evolved prior to the divergence of sponges and eumetazoans.
source: These results suggest that the regulatory foundation for spatiotemporal gene expression evolved prior to the divergence of sponges and eumetazoans, and was necessary for the evolution of animal multicellularity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: The regulatory foundation for spatiotemporal gene expression was necessary for the evolution of animal multicellularity.
source: These results suggest that the regulatory foundation for spatiotemporal gene expression evolved prior to the divergence of sponges and eumetazoans, and was necessary for the evolution of animal multicellularity.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the evolutionary role of regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The last common ancestor of modern animals already possessed an extensive repertoire of regulatory genes, including most transcription factors and signaling pathways used in bilaterian development.
source: As the last common ancestor of modern animals already possessed an extensive repertoire of regulatory genes, including most transcription factors and signaling pathways used in bilaterian development (Srivastava et al., 2010; Larroux et al., 2008; Degnan et al., 2009; Larroux et al., 2006; Richards and Degnan, 2009; Ryan et al., 2013; Moroz et al., 2014; King et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2011; de Mendoza et al., 2013; King et al., 2003; Richter and King, 2013), the evolution of animal multicellularity likely required more than the origin of novel genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The evolution of animal multicellularity likely required more than the origin of novel genes.
source: As the last common ancestor of modern animals already possessed an extensive repertoire of regulatory genes, including most transcription factors and signaling pathways used in bilaterian development (Srivastava et al., 2010; Larroux et al., 2008; Degnan et al., 2009; Larroux et al., 2006; Richards and Degnan, 2009; Ryan et al., 2013; Moroz et al., 2014; King et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2011; de Mendoza et al., 2013; King et al., 2003; Richter and King, 2013), the evolution of animal multicellularity likely required more than the origin of novel genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of regulatory genes in the last common ancestor.

claim: Cis-regulatory DNA and combinatorial patterns of histone covalent post-translational modifications would have been instrumental to direct differential gene expression in the first multicellular animals.
source: Other regulatory features, such as cis-regulatory DNA and combinatorial patterns of histone covalent post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Davidson and Peter, 2015), would have been instrumental to direct differential gene expression in the first multicellular animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the role of regulatory features in early animal evolution, supported by a citation.

claim: Capsaspora, one of the closest unicellular relatives of animals, reveals a lack of chromatin repressive marks, developmental promoter types and distal cis-regulatory elements (enhancers) typically present in complex animals.
source: For instance, recent analysis of the genome of Capsaspora, one of the closest unicellular relatives of animals, reveals a lack of chromatin repressive marks, developmental promoter types and distal cis-regulatory elements (enhancers) typically present in complex animals (i.e., eumetazoans) (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on Capsaspora.

claim: Combinatorial patterns of histone acetylation and methylation are key components of gene regulatory mechanisms underpinning the formation and maintenance of eumetazoans.
source: Although combinatorial patterns of histone acetylation and methylation are key components of gene regulatory mechanisms underpinning the formation and maintenance of eumetazoans (Schwaiger et al., 2014), it remains unknown if this system is restricted to these animals or is indeed more ancient.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It remains unknown if the system of combinatorial histone modifications is restricted to eumetazoans or is more ancient.
source: Although combinatorial patterns of histone acetylation and methylation are key components of gene regulatory mechanisms underpinning the formation and maintenance of eumetazoans (Schwaiger et al., 2014), it remains unknown if this system is restricted to these animals or is indeed more ancient.
evidence: This is a statement of the research question addressed by the study.

claim: Amphimedon adults and larvae are comprised of different cell types with markedly different transcriptional profiles and regulatory states.
source: Importantly, Amphimedon adults and larvae are comprised of different cell types with markedly different transcriptional profiles and regulatory states (Gaiti et al., 2015; Conaco et al., 2012; Fernandez-Valverde et al., 2015; Degnan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Amphimedon genome is a draft sequence with incomplete annotations and gaps in the assembly (13% of the total genome assembly).
source: Given the current Amphimedon genome is a draft sequence, our analyses may also be incomplete in regions that have incomplete annotations and gaps in the assembly (13% of the total genome assembly) (Srivastava et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the genome assembly, supported by a citation.

claim: The entire amino acid sequence of histone H3 is perfectly conserved in Amphimedon.
source: As the entire amino acid sequence of histone H3 is perfectly conserved in Amphimedon, along with the relevant histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, these antibodies are predicted to recognize the correct epitopes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—source data 2; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a figure showing sequence conservation.

claim: The relevant histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases are conserved in Amphimedon.
source: As the entire amino acid sequence of histone H3 is perfectly conserved in Amphimedon, along with the relevant histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, these antibodies are predicted to recognize the correct epitopes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—source data 2; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to source data showing conservation of these enzymes.

claim: Nine chromatin states were identified in Amphimedon that fell into two broad categories: one correlated with actively transcribed genes and another with genes with no or little detectable transcription.
source: Despite the inherent cellular heterogeneity of our starting material, we were able to resolve specificities towards gene components between these nine chromatin states. They fell into two broad categories: one that correlated with actively transcribed genes that include active promoters ('TssA') and enhancers ('TxEnhA', 'EnhWk'), and 5' and 3' boundaries of transcribed genes ('TxFlnk'); and another category with genes with no or little detectable transcription; these include bivalent or poised regulatory ('BivTx', 'EnhP'), repressed Polycomb ('ReprPC', 'ReprPCWk'), and quiescent ('Quies') states (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ChromHMM analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The 'TssA' state (defined by the presence of H3K4me3) was enriched around transcription start sites (TSSs) of active genes.
source: For instance, the 'TssA' state (defined by the presence of H3K4me3) was enriched around transcription start sites (TSSs) of active genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the ChromHMM analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: 'TxEnhA' state (defined by H3K4me1, H3K27ac, and H3K36me3 enrichment) associated with coding exons and introns that correspond to potential cis-regulatory elements and short intergenic regions.
source: 'TxEnhA' state (defined by H3K4me1, H3K27ac, and H3K36me3 enrichment) associated with coding exons and introns that correspond to potential cis-regulatory elements and short intergenic regions, which are common in the Amphimedon genome (Kundaje et al., 2015; Fernandez-Valverde et al., 2015; Kowalczyk et al., 2012; Ritter et al., 2012; Singer et al., 2015; Birnbaum et al., 2012; Zentner and Scacheri, 2012; Zentner et al., 2011; Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChromHMM analysis, supported by citations to prior research on enhancers and the Amphimedon genome.

claim: The 'ReprPC' states (defined by H3K27me3 enrichment) were spread through the gene bodies of repressed genes, consistent with the known role of H3K27me3 in transcriptional silencing.
source: In contrast, the 'ReprPC' states (defined by H3K27me3 enrichment) were spread through the gene bodies of repressed genes, consistent with the known role of H3K27me3 in transcriptional silencing (Zhou et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014) (Figure 1BD; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChromHMM analysis, supported by citations to prior research on H3K27me3 function.

claim: The larval genome possesses a remarkably similar set of chromatin states to the adult genome.
source: Despite being comprised of different cell types and having a distinct gene expression profile from the adult, the larval genome possesses a remarkably similar set of chromatin states (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChromHMM analysis of larval ChIP-seq data.

claim: A strong unimodal H3K4me3 peak positioned immediately after the TSS of expressed genes co-localizes with H3K27ac and RNAPII.
source: Input-normalized ChIP-seq read coverage revealed a strong unimodal H3K4me3 peak positioned immediately after the TSS of expressed genes that co-localizes with H3K27ac and RNAPII (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: H3K4me3 marked genes with head-to-head orientation that may be under the control of a bidirectional promoter.
source: Additionally, H3K4me3 marked (i) genes with head-to-head orientation that may be under the control of a bidirectional promoter (a common feature in the Amphimedon genome [Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016]), and (ii) alternative TSSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data, supported by a citation about bidirectional promoters in Amphimedon.

claim: H3K4me3 marked alternative TSSs.
source: Additionally, H3K4me3 marked (i) genes with head-to-head orientation that may be under the control of a bidirectional promoter (a common feature in the Amphimedon genome [Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016]), and (ii) alternative TSSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: A prominent nucleosome-depleted region was observed right upstream of the TSS of expressed genes.
source: A prominent nucleosome-depleted region was observed right upstream of the TSS of expressed genes (likely corresponding to the proximal promoter) followed by a narrowly localized nucleosome (the +1 nucleosome) (see below Figure 2—figure supplement 4D), suggesting that the interplay between nucleosome positioning and transcription is conserved in sponge promoters (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Schwaiger et al., 2014; Roy et al., 2010; Bai and Morozov, 2010; Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of total histone H3 ChIP-seq data, supported by citations to prior research on nucleosome positioning.

claim: The interplay between nucleosome positioning and transcription is conserved in sponge promoters.
source: A prominent nucleosome-depleted region was observed right upstream of the TSS of expressed genes (likely corresponding to the proximal promoter) followed by a narrowly localized nucleosome (the +1 nucleosome) (see below Figure 2—figure supplement 4D), suggesting that the interplay between nucleosome positioning and transcription is conserved in sponge promoters (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Schwaiger et al., 2014; Roy et al., 2010; Bai and Morozov, 2010; Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of nucleosome depletion, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The distribution of histone H3 PTMs in Amphimedon correlated with the expression state of its genes.
source: Overall, the distribution of histone H3 PTMs in Amphimedon correlated with the expression state of its genes, as in eumetazoans (Schwaiger et al., 2014; Roy et al., 2010) (Fisher's exact test, FDR adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data, supported by statistical testing and citations to prior research.

claim: High-variance genes were strongly marked by H3K4me3 and occupied by RNAPII.
source: The TSSs of high-variance genes were strongly marked by H3K4me3 and occupied by RNAPII (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data for high-variance genes.

claim: High-variance genes showed nucleosome depletion right upstream of the TSSs.
source: Additionally, they showed nucleosome depletion right upstream of the TSSs (seen as lack of total histone H3 signal), consistent with the notion that H3K4me3 near TSSs destabilizes the interaction between histones and DNA to direct RNAPII to facilitate binding of promoter regulator elements and initiate transcription (Jiang and Pugh, 2009; Ha et al., 2011; Boeger et al., 2003) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of total histone H3 ChIP-seq data, supported by citations to prior research on H3K4me3 function.

claim: Low-variance genes had lower levels of H3K4me3 or RNAPII but higher nucleosome occupancy compared to high-variance genes.
source: Conversely, lower levels of H3K4me3 or RNAPII (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=0.05287 and p-value<2.2e-16, respectively; Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 4C) but higher nucleosome occupancy characterized low-variance genes (seen as lack of nucleosome depletion right upstream of the TSSs; Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data, supported by statistical testing.

claim: H3K4me3 is predictive of gene expression levels.
source: These results are consistent with H3K4me3 being predictive of gene expression levels (Ha et al., 2011; Karlić et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-variance genes were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways.
source: High-variance genes, which also include a significantly higher number of transcription factor gene families (e.g., JUN and ATF6 Jindrich and Degnan [2016]) compared to low-variance genes (Fisher's exact test, p-value=3.872e-08), were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways (Hypergeometric test, FDR adjusted p-value<0.01; Figure 2E; see Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 2 for the complete list).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analyses, supported by statistical testing.

claim: High-variance genes include a significantly higher number of transcription factor gene families compared to low-variance genes.
source: High-variance genes, which also include a significantly higher number of transcription factor gene families (e.g., JUN and ATF6 Jindrich and Degnan [2016]) compared to low-variance genes (Fisher's exact test, p-value=3.872e-08), were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways (Hypergeometric test, FDR adjusted p-value<0.01; Figure 2E; see Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 2 for the complete list).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of gene families, supported by statistical testing.

claim: Low-variance genes were enriched for metabolic GO terms.
source: In contrast, low-variance genes were enriched for metabolic GO terms (Figure 2E; see Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 2 for the complete list).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis.

claim: H3K4me3 is important for tuning the gene expression of dynamically expressed developmental genes.
source: This result is consistent with H3K4me3 being important for tuning the gene expression of dynamically expressed developmental genes, e.g., transcription factor and signaling genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of high-variance genes in signaling pathways and transcription factors.

claim: It remains unclear whether H3K4me3 is needed for high levels of gene expression or if it is needed for, or associated with, frequent switching of transcriptional status.
source: However, it remains unclear whether H3K4me3 is needed for high levels of gene expression or if it is needed for, or associated with, frequent switching of transcriptional status.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Transcription of a subpopulation of extremely dynamically expressed genes in Drosophila and C. elegans occurs in the absence of H3K4me3.
source: The recent finding that transcription of a subpopulation of extremely dynamically expressed genes – typically being expressed at only one stage of development – in Drosophila and C. elegans occurs in the absence of H3K4me3 challenged the canonical role of histone PTMs in the modulation of gene expression (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Stable genes were strongly marked by H3K4me3 and regulated genes had significantly lower levels of H3K4me3.
source: Although stable and regulated genes had similar levels of RNAPII and total histone H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C ), the stable genes were strongly marked by H3K4me3 and the regulated genes had significantly lower levels of H3K4me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=7.431e-05; Figure 3A), suggesting that reduction in H3K4me3 levels does not affect expression of the regulated genes (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data for stable and regulated genes, supported by statistical testing and a citation.

claim: Reduction in H3K4me3 levels does not affect expression of the regulated genes.
source: Although stable and regulated genes had similar levels of RNAPII and total histone H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C ), the stable genes were strongly marked by H3K4me3 and the regulated genes had significantly lower levels of H3K4me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=7.431e-05; Figure 3A), suggesting that reduction in H3K4me3 levels does not affect expression of the regulated genes (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that regulated genes have low H3K4me3 but are still expressed, supported by a citation.

claim: Regulated genes showed higher levels of H3K27me3 than stable genes.
source: Additionally, as shown in Drosophila (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a), regulated genes showed higher levels of H3K27me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<6.517e-06) and lower levels of H3K36me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<9.235e-08) than did stable genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data, supported by statistical testing and a citation.

claim: Regulated genes showed lower levels of H3K36me3 than stable genes.
source: Additionally, as shown in Drosophila (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a), regulated genes showed higher levels of H3K27me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<6.517e-06) and lower levels of H3K36me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<9.235e-08) than did stable genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ChIP-seq data, supported by statistical testing and a citation.

claim: The same pattern of H3K4me3 in stable and regulated genes was observed in Nematostella vectensis.
source: Analyzing RNA-seq–based gene expression through the development of the cnidarian Nematostella vectensis (Helm et al., 2013) and previously published ChIP-seq data sets in Nematostella adult female polyps (Schwaiger et al., 2014), we obtained the same pattern (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<2.2e-16; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Nematostella data, supported by statistical testing and citations.

claim: H3K4me3 might not be instrumental for extremely dynamic developmental expression.
source: These results suggest that H3K4me3 might not be instrumental for extremely dynamic developmental expression and enforces our interpretation that it is required for tuning the levels of gene expression, a pattern that appears to be a conserved metazoan feature (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: H3K4me3 is required for tuning the levels of gene expression, a pattern that appears to be a conserved metazoan feature.
source: These results suggest that H3K4me3 might not be instrumental for extremely dynamic developmental expression and enforces our interpretation that it is required for tuning the levels of gene expression, a pattern that appears to be a conserved metazoan feature (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: PRC2 is responsible for the trimethylation of lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3).
source: PRC2 is responsible for the trimethylation of lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3), one of the best-characterized repressive histone H3 PTMs (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC2 function, supported by a citation.

claim: The Amphimedon genome contains four copies of E(z) homologs, two copies of ESC homologs and one copy for each of the remaining components, SU(z)12 and Nurf55.
source: As a step to investigate a putative mechanism of PRC2-mediated silencing in Amphimedon, we identified the sponge homologs of Drosophila PRC2 components and found that the Amphimedon genome contains four copies of E(z) homologs, two copies of ESC homologs and one copy for each of the remaining components, SU(z)12 and Nurf55 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the identification of PRC2 homologs in the Amphimedon genome.

claim: Conserved binding motifs similar to the GAGA and Krüppel-like factors were significantly enriched in the DNA associated with the H3K27me3 silenced regions in both adult and larva.
source: Conserved binding motifs similar to the GAGA and Krüppel-like factors, in addition to binding motifs similar to homeodomain-containing developmental regulators (e.g., Irx family members), were significantly enriched (E-value<0.05) in the DNA associated with the H3K27me3 silenced regions in both adult and larva (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from de novo motif analysis of H3K27me3 regions.

claim: Binding motifs similar to homeodomain-containing developmental regulators were significantly enriched in the DNA associated with the H3K27me3 silenced regions in both adult and larva.
source: Conserved binding motifs similar to the GAGA and Krüppel-like factors, in addition to binding motifs similar to homeodomain-containing developmental regulators (e.g., Irx family members), were significantly enriched (E-value<0.05) in the DNA associated with the H3K27me3 silenced regions in both adult and larva (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from de novo motif analysis of H3K27me3 regions.

claim: Amphimedon PRC2 complexes are likely to be recruited through PRE-like sequences and may target developmental regulators for H3K27me3 deposition and transcriptional silencing.
source: As in eumetazoans, this result suggests that Amphimedon PRC2 complexes are likely to be recruited through PRE-like sequences and may target developmental regulators for H3K27me3 deposition and transcriptional silencing (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of transcription factor binding motifs in H3K27me3 regions, supported by citations.

claim: Long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) have been demonstrated to be developmentally expressed in sponges.
source: An additional layer of regulatory complexity in eumetazoan development is provided by long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) (Ulitsky, 2016; Hezroni et al., 2015; Quinn and Chang, 2016), which have been recently demonstrated to be developmentally expressed in sponges (Gaiti et al., 2015; Bråte et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ratio of H3K4me1-to-H3K4me3 marks around TSSs can separate lincRNAs into enhancer-like lincRNAs (elincRNAs) and canonical promoter-like lincRNAs (plincRNAs).
source: Previous studies have shown that the ratio of H3K4me1-to-H3K4me3 marks around TSSs can separate lincRNAs into enhancer-like lincRNAs (elincRNAs; high H3K4me1-to-H3K4me3 ratio) and canonical promoter-like lincRNAs (plincRNAs; low H3K4me1-to-H3K4me3 ratio) (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Marques et al., 2013; IIott et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 153 putative elincRNAs (70%) were found in Amphimedon, significantly enriched for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3.
source: Based on these criteria, we found 153 putative elincRNAs (70%) significantly enriched for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=2.272e-05) and 21 (10%) putative plincRNAs with canonical promoter signature, i.e., higher enrichment of H3K4me3 over H3K4me1 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=1.925e-07).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of lincRNA chromatin states, supported by statistical testing.

claim: 21 (10%) putative plincRNAs with canonical promoter signature were found in Amphimedon.
source: Based on these criteria, we found 153 putative elincRNAs (70%) significantly enriched for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=2.272e-05) and 21 (10%) putative plincRNAs with canonical promoter signature, i.e., higher enrichment of H3K4me3 over H3K4me1 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=1.925e-07).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of lincRNA chromatin states, supported by statistical testing.

claim: Sponge lincRNAs can be separated in two distinct populations of poly(A)+ transcripts based on the chromatin status at their TSSs.
source: These results indicate that sponge lincRNAs can be separated in two distinct populations of poly(A)+ transcripts based on the chromatin status at their TSSs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the identification of elincRNAs and plincRNAs.

claim: The two populations of sponge lincRNAs resemble those found in human, mouse and Capsaspora lincRNAs.
source: Although these two populations resemble those found in human, mouse and Capsaspora lincRNAs (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Marques et al., 2013; IIott et al., 2014), their functional significance is yet to be determined.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Predicted activated enhancer-like regions showed a significant enrichment of H3K4me1 and H3K27ac over H3K4me3.
source: These predicted activated enhancer-like regions showed a significant enrichment of H3K4me1 and H3K27ac over H3K4me3 (Mann-Whitney U test, p-value<2.2e-16; Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), a biochemical signature typical of eumetazoan enhancers (Schwaiger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of predicted enhancer regions, supported by statistical testing and a citation.

claim: RNAPII occupied some of the Amphimedon predicted activated enhancer-like elements (35% and 41% in adult and larva, respectively).
source: Interestingly, RNAPII occupied some of these Amphimedon predicted activated enhancer-like elements (35% and 41% in adult and larva, respectively), suggesting poly(A)+ enhancer RNAs could be transcribed from these regions (Natoli and Andrau, 2012; Li et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010) (Figure 6A–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of RNAPII ChIP-seq data at enhancer regions, supported by citations.

claim: Poly(A)+ enhancer RNAs could be transcribed from Amphimedon predicted activated enhancer-like elements.
source: Interestingly, RNAPII occupied some of these Amphimedon predicted activated enhancer-like elements (35% and 41% in adult and larva, respectively), suggesting poly(A)+ enhancer RNAs could be transcribed from these regions (Natoli and Andrau, 2012; Li et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010) (Figure 6A–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of RNAPII at enhancer regions, supported by citations.

claim: RNAPII occupancy at enhancers might represent the result of chromatin looping and the simultaneous pulldown of both enhancers and promoters with the RNAPII antibody.
source: Alternatively, but not exclusively, this might represent the result of chromatin looping and the simultaneous pulldown of both enhancers and promoters with the RNAPII antibody (Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation about the RNAPII signal at enhancers, supported by a citation.

claim: Consensus binding motifs of key developmental transcription factor families were over-represented in the adult predicted activated enhancer-like sequences.
source: We therefore performed de novo motif analysis and, despite the limited power of motif detection due to the inherent cellular heterogeneity of our starting material, we were able to show that consensus binding motifs of key developmental transcription factor families were over-represented in the adult predicted activated enhancer-like sequences, including Zinc finger, Irx, SOX and POU binding motifs (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from de novo motif analysis of enhancer sequences.

claim: Nearest neighbor genes to predicted activated enhancer-like elements were significantly enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) terms associated with transcription factor activity and developmental processes.
source: By searching for the closest located TSSs to each of the predicted activated enhancer-like elements in Amphimedon, we nominated putative target protein-coding genes. Akin to eumetazoans, these nearest neighbor genes were significantly enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) terms associated with transcription factor activity and developmental processes (Hypergeometric test, FDR adjusted p-value<0.01) (Figure 6F), and comprised several transcription factors, including SOX2, FOS and NF-kB (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 5; Figure 6—source data 2–5).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis of genes near enhancers, supported by statistical testing.

claim: Nearest neighbor genes to predicted activated enhancer-like elements comprised several transcription factors, including SOX2, FOS and NF-kB.
source: By searching for the closest located TSSs to each of the predicted activated enhancer-like elements in Amphimedon, we nominated putative target protein-coding genes. Akin to eumetazoans, these nearest neighbor genes were significantly enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) terms associated with transcription factor activity and developmental processes (Hypergeometric test, FDR adjusted p-value<0.01) (Figure 6F), and comprised several transcription factors, including SOX2, FOS and NF-kB (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 5; Figure 6—source data 2–5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of genes near enhancers.

claim: Predicted activated enhancer-like elements were predominantly intragenic in Amphimedon, with only a minority found in intergenic regions (9% and 20% in adult and larva, respectively).
source: In contrast, in Amphimedon, which has a highly compact genome with minimal intergenic regions (Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016), predicted activated enhancer-like elements were predominantly intragenic, with only a minority found in intergenic regions (9% and 20% in adult and larva, respectively) (Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of enhancer locations, supported by a citation.

claim: The genomic distribution of Amphimedon enhancer elements is similar to Nematostella and Drosophila enhancer elements.
source: This, along with the strong enrichment of chromatin states typically associated with eumetazoan enhancers – 'TxEnhA' and 'EnhWk' – in introns (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggests a similar overall genomic distribution between Amphimedon, Nematostella and Drosophila enhancer elements (Schwaiger et al., 2014; Nègre et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the intragenic location of enhancers, supported by citations.

claim: Introns that harbour predicted activated enhancer-like elements were significantly longer than the average genomic intron size.
source: We, therefore, extracted the introns that harbour predicted activated enhancer-like elements and compared their size distribution to the size of all intronic regions found across the genome. The former were significantly longer than the average genomic intron size, with a mean of 332 bp and 256 bp, and a median of 99 bp and 71 bp, respectively (Ansari-Bradley test, p-value=0.06151; Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=1.927e-06) (Figure 6G), suggesting that a cis-regulatory expansion appear to have occurred primarily in intronic rather than intergenic regions in Amphimedon.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of intron sizes, supported by statistical testing.

claim: A cis-regulatory expansion appear to have occurred primarily in intronic rather than intergenic regions in Amphimedon.
source: We, therefore, extracted the introns that harbour predicted activated enhancer-like elements and compared their size distribution to the size of all intronic regions found across the genome. The former were significantly longer than the average genomic intron size, with a mean of 332 bp and 256 bp, and a median of 99 bp and 71 bp, respectively (Ansari-Bradley test, p-value=0.06151; Mann-Whitney U test, p-value=1.927e-06) (Figure 6G), suggesting that a cis-regulatory expansion appear to have occurred primarily in intronic rather than intergenic regions in Amphimedon.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that introns with enhancers are longer.

claim: 43 of 60 evolutionary conserved metazoan microsyntenies contained putative enhancer-like signatures in Amphimedon adults.
source: Remarkably, 43 of these 60 evolutionary conserved metazoan microsyntenies contained putative enhancer-like signatures in Amphimedon adults (Figure 7A; Figure 7—source data 1; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of microsyntenic units and enhancer locations.

claim: The fraction of microsyntenic units with enhancer-like signatures was much higher relative to a control set consisting of 60 pairs of two randomly selected nonsyntenic neighbor genes.
source: This was a much higher fraction relative to a control set consisting of 60 pairs of two randomly selected nonsyntenic neighbor genes (1,000 iterations; p-value<0.00001).
evidence: This is a finding from a statistical comparison to a control set.

claim: 16 of the 60 microsyntenic units contained larva enhancer-like signatures, seven of which contained both larva and adult predicted enhancer-like elements.
source: This pattern was substantiated by the finding of larva enhancer-like signatures in 16 of the 60 microsyntenic units, seven of which contained both larva and adult predicted enhancer-like elements (Figure 7A; Figure 7—source data 1; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of microsyntenic units and enhancer locations in larva.

claim: The Isl-Scaper microsyntenic gene pair is deeply conserved.
source: A striking case of conserved gene linkage involves the Islet LIM homeobox gene (Isl), which plays conserved roles in animal development (Thor and Thomas, 1997; Liang et al., 2011), and Scaper (S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the ER) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of microsynteny, supported by citations about Isl function.

claim: The Amphimedon Scaper contains 25 introns, some of which are considerably longer (>1 kb) than the mean intron size.
source: The Amphimedon Scaper contains 25 introns, some of which are considerably longer (>1 kb) than the mean intron size (Fernandez-Valverde et al., 2015), and predicted enhancer-like elements located within its intron 10, 17 and 21 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the Scaper gene structure and enhancer locations, supported by a citation.

claim: Predicted enhancer-like elements are located within intron 10, 17 and 21 of Amphimedon Scaper.
source: The Amphimedon Scaper contains 25 introns, some of which are considerably longer (>1 kb) than the mean intron size (Fernandez-Valverde et al., 2015), and predicted enhancer-like elements located within its intron 10, 17 and 21 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of enhancer locations in the Scaper gene.

claim: The microsynteny of Tfap4 and Glis2 is deeply conserved.
source: Likewise, the microsynteny of Tfap4 (transcription factor AP-4) (Simionato et al., 2007) and Glis2 (GLIS family zinc finger 2) is deeply conserved.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of microsynteny, supported by a citation.

claim: The sponge Glis2 contains two introns, of which the second harbors several adult predicted activated enhancer-like elements.
source: Similar to an observation in vertebrates (Abbasi et al., 2007), the sponge Glis2 contains two introns, of which the second harbors several adult predicted activated enhancer-like elements (Figure 7—source data 1; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the Glis2 gene structure and enhancer locations, supported by a citation.

claim: The genomic location of some cis-regulatory elements likely places constraints on the evolution of nearby genes, leading to the occurrence of conserved microsyntenic gene blocks across the animal kingdom.
source: Together, these results suggest that the genomic location of some cis-regulatory elements likely places constraints on the evolution of nearby genes, leading to the occurrence of conserved microsyntenic gene blocks across the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of enhancers in microsyntenic units.

claim: Sponges and eumetazoans have had radically different evolutionary histories since their point of divergence over 700 Mya.
source: Since their point of divergence over 700 Mya, sponges and eumetazoans have had radically different evolutionary histories, with the eumetazoan ancestor giving rise to a range of morphologically-complex body plans, and the sponge ancestor yielding one basic morphologically-simple body plan.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about animal evolution.

claim: Amphimedon displays dynamic developmental gene expression akin to eumetazoans.
source: Recently it has been shown that, despite having a highly compact genome with minimal intergenic regions (Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016), Amphimedon displays dynamic developmental gene expression akin to eumetazoans (Gaiti et al., 2015; Levin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This study generated the first comprehensive genome-wide maps of histone H3 PTMs and putative enhancer elements in a non-eumetazoan animal.
source: By generating the first, to our knowledge, comprehensive genome-wide maps of histone H3 PTMs and putative enhancer elements in a non-eumetazoan animal, we determine that this transcriptional complexity is paralleled by regulatory complexity encoded by combinatorial histone H3 PTM patterns in this sponge.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study.

claim: The genome-wide promoter analysis of H3K4me3 reveals a complex correlation between H3K4me3-containing nucleosome occupancy and gene expression in Amphimedon adults and larvae.
source: For instance, the genome-wide promoter analysis of H3K4me3 – the canonical and widespread eukaryotic histone H3 PTM of active transcription – reveals a complex correlation between H3K4me3-containing nucleosome occupancy and gene expression in Amphimedon adults and larvae, consistent with an active and finely tuned role for H3K4me3 in modulating transcriptional activity and expression variability of developmental genes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the H3K4me3 analysis.

claim: A small subpopulation of highly and specifically expressed genes are transcribed in the absence of H3K4me3 in Amphimedon and Nematostella.
source: Unexpectedly, we identify a small subpopulation of highly and specifically expressed genes that challenge this premise and are transcribed in the absence of H3K4me3 in Amphimedon and Nematostella.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about regulated genes.

claim: The absence of H3K4me3 in regulated genes would allow their rapid on-off switching.
source: As the expression of the developmentally regulated genes is required only for a limited period, the absence of H3K4me3 mark would allow their rapid on-off switching.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the absence of H3K4me3.

claim: Alternative mechanisms, such as the transient binding of transcription factors, appear to play a major role in regulating the expression of regulated genes.
source: Alternative mechanisms, such as the transient binding of transcription factors, appear to play a major role in regulating the expression of these genes (Pérez-Lluch et al., 2015a, 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) has been conserved throughout opisthokonts evolution, with its core subunits being present in animals, choanoflagellates and multicellular fungi, but absent in Capsaspora, and budding and fission yeast.
source: Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) primarily trimethylates histone H3 on lysine 27 and has been conserved throughout opisthokonts evolution, with its core subunits (E(z), SU(z)12, ESC and Nurf55) being present in animals, choanoflagellates and multicellular fungi, but absent in Capsaspora, and budding and fission yeast (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Shaver et al., 2010; Jamieson et al., 2013; Connolly et al., 2013; Ikeuchi et al., 2015; Whitcomb et al., 2007) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRC2 complex has been lost in several unicellular lineages.
source: This is consistent with PRC2 complex being lost in several unicellular lineages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic distribution of PRC2.

claim: One of the ancestral roles of PCR2 in opisthokonts may have been in defense response against viruses and transposable elements, or insertion of new genes.
source: One of the ancestral roles of PCR2 in opisthokonts may have been in defense response against viruses and transposable elements, or insertion of new genes (Jamieson et al., 2013), prior to being co-opted for cell-type specific developmental regulation in animals, where H3K27me3 and PRC2 are required for transmitting the memory of repression across generations and during development (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Shaver et al., 2010; Gaydos et al., 2014; Barski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation about the ancestral function of PRC2, supported by citations.

claim: PRC2 was co-opted for cell-type specific developmental regulation in animals.
source: One of the ancestral roles of PCR2 in opisthokonts may have been in defense response against viruses and transposable elements, or insertion of new genes (Jamieson et al., 2013), prior to being co-opted for cell-type specific developmental regulation in animals, where H3K27me3 and PRC2 are required for transmitting the memory of repression across generations and during development (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Shaver et al., 2010; Gaydos et al., 2014; Barski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolution of PRC2 function, supported by citations.

claim: H3K27me3 and PRC2 are required for transmitting the memory of repression across generations and during development in animals.
source: One of the ancestral roles of PCR2 in opisthokonts may have been in defense response against viruses and transposable elements, or insertion of new genes (Jamieson et al., 2013), prior to being co-opted for cell-type specific developmental regulation in animals, where H3K27me3 and PRC2 are required for transmitting the memory of repression across generations and during development (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Shaver et al., 2010; Gaydos et al., 2014; Barski et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRC2 often regulates deposition of H3K27me3 marks at loci encoding developmental regulators.
source: In fact, PRC2 often regulates deposition of H3K27me3 marks at loci encoding developmental regulators (Ha et al., 2011; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Barski et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The identification of an enriched motif in the H3K27me3 silenced regions similar to the GAGA factor binding site suggests a role for the GAGA factor binding sites in strengthening PRC2 recruitment to target genes.
source: Analogous to recent findings in plants (Deng et al., 2013; Hecker et al., 2015), the identification of an enriched motif in the H3K27me3 silenced regions similar to the GAGA factor binding site, a component of the Drosophila Polycomb group response elements, suggests a role for the GAGA factor binding sites in strengthening PRC2 recruitment to target genes (Müller and Kassis, 2006; Simon and Kingston, 2009; Kassis and Brown, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motif enrichment, supported by citations.

claim: A sponge homolog of Drosophila GAGA factor was not identified in the current Amphimedon genome assembly.
source: It is noteworthy that a sponge homolog of Drosophila GAGA factor was not identified in the current Amphimedon genome assembly (Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting the convergent co-option of other DNA binding proteins with analogous role(s) in the recruitment of PRC2.
evidence: This is a finding from the search for GAGA factor homologs.

claim: The absence of a GAGA factor homolog suggests the convergent co-option of other DNA binding proteins with analogous role(s) in the recruitment of PRC2.
source: It is noteworthy that a sponge homolog of Drosophila GAGA factor was not identified in the current Amphimedon genome assembly (Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting the convergent co-option of other DNA binding proteins with analogous role(s) in the recruitment of PRC2.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of PRC2 recruitment in Amphimedon.

claim: Some cis-regulatory mechanisms, such as those associated with proximal promoters, are present in non-animal holozoans.
source: Analysis of cis-regulatory DNA and histone PTMs have revealed that some cis-regulatory mechanisms, such as those associated with proximal promoters, are present in non-animal holozoans, while others appear to have evolved later on the stem leading to the crown metazoans, most notably distal enhancers (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Schwaiger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distal enhancers appear to have evolved on the stem leading to the crown metazoans.
source: Analysis of cis-regulatory DNA and histone PTMs have revealed that some cis-regulatory mechanisms, such as those associated with proximal promoters, are present in non-animal holozoans, while others appear to have evolved later on the stem leading to the crown metazoans, most notably distal enhancers (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Schwaiger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distal enhancers have been posited to be one of the key contributing factors underlying the spatial and temporal coordination of cell differentiation that defines animal development.
source: The latter has been posited to be one of the key contributing factors underlying the spatial and temporal coordination of cell differentiation that defines animal development (Levine, 2010; Levine et al., 2014; Levine and Tjian, 2003; Peter and Davidson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The in silico prediction of Amphimedon enhancer elements based on histone H3 PTM co-localization patterns is consistent with these elements evolving along the metazoan stem at the transition to multicellularity.
source: Our in silico prediction of Amphimedon enhancer elements based on histone H3 PTM co-localization patterns is consistent with these elements evolving along the metazoan stem at the transition to multicellularity (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the identification of enhancers in Amphimedon, supported by a citation.

claim: Promoter DNA regulatory elements to allow for context and cell type-specific gene expression appeared to evolve in stem metazoans.
source: Interestingly, promoter DNA regulatory elements to allow for context and cell type-specific gene expression also appeared to evolve in stem metazoans (Fernandez-Valverde and Degnan, 2016), suggesting these are also a critical component of the animal cis-regulatory landscape.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Amphimedon predicted enhancer-like elements are characterized by the same combination of histone H3 PTMs as in eumetazoans, which appear to be lacking in unicellular holozoan relatives of animals.
source: Amphimedon predicted enhancer-like elements are characterized by the same combination of histone H3 PTMs as in eumetazoans, which appear to be lacking in unicellular holozoan relatives of animals (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Bulger and Groudine, 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of enhancer chromatin states, supported by citations.

claim: The preferential association of Amphimedon enhancer elements with developmental and transcriptional regulators suggests that they are likely to regulate developmental genes in a manner akin to eumetazoans.
source: Their preferential association with developmental and transcriptional regulators suggests that Amphimedon enhancer elements are likely to regulate developmental genes in a manner akin to eumetazoans (Schwaiger et al., 2014; Shlyueva et al., 2014; Nègre et al., 2011; Bogdanovic et al., 2012; Woolfe et al., 2005; Heintzman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GO enrichment analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Enhancer elements are known to be associated with the transcription of both short poly(A)- and long poly(A)+ enhancer RNAs.
source: Enhancer elements are known to be associated with the transcription of both short poly(A)- and long poly(A)+ enhancer RNAs (2D and 1D eRNAs, respectively) (Natoli and Andrau, 2012; Li et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about enhancers, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of RNAPII and the detection of expression at a subset of the Amphimedon activated enhancer-like elements is consistent with the transcription of enhancer RNAs.
source: The presence of RNAPII and the detection of expression at a subset of the Amphimedon activated enhancer-like elements is consistent with this notion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of RNAPII at enhancers.

claim: The co-occupancy of enhancer elements and RNAPII has been observed in Nematostella and bilaterians.
source: Although non-coding transcription at these enhancers will need to be investigated in detail, this co-occupancy of enhancer elements and RNAPII has also been observed in Nematostella and bilaterians (Schwaiger et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010; De Santa et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013), where these elements might be physically interacting with the transcription initiation complex at the TSS of their target gene(s) (Schwaiger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Amphimedon lacks CTCF.
source: Unlike bilaterians, where the transcriptional repressor CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) localizes with cohesin genome-wide and is involved in enhancer-promoter long-range interactions and higher-order chromatin structure (Lee and Iyer, 2012; Seitan et al., 2013; Merkenschlager and Odom, 2013), Amphimedon lacks CTCF (Heger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The absence of CTCF likely constrains Amphimedon enhancer interactions with the proximal promoter transcriptional machinery to short distances.
source: This likely constrains Amphimedon enhancer interactions with the proximal promoter transcriptional machinery to short distances.
evidence: This is a speculation about the consequences of lacking CTCF.

claim: Chromatin looping of enhancers to their target promoters in Amphimedon might occur through a CTCF-independent cohesin binding mechanism.
source: Chromatin looping of enhancers to their target promoters in this sponge might therefore occur through a CTCF-independent cohesin binding mechanism, as proposed in cnidarians, which also lack CTCF (Schwaiger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhancer-promoter interaction, supported by a citation.

claim: RNAPII and its associated transcriptional machinery may track through the intervening DNA between enhancers and promoters, and might be the preferred mechanism of enhancer-promoter interactions in Amphimedon.
source: Alternatively, but not exclusively, RNAPII and its associated transcriptional machinery may track through the intervening DNA between enhancers and promoters (Li et al., 2016), and might be the preferred mechanism of enhancer-promoter interactions in this sponge.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhancer-promoter interaction, supported by a citation.

claim: The co-occupancy of Amphimedon enhancer-like elements and RNAPII supports the mechanism of transcriptional activation by RNAPII tracking.
source: The co-occupancy of Amphimedon enhancer-like elements and RNAPII supports this mechanism of transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of RNAPII at enhancers.

claim: There is strong evidence for cis-regulatory elements being important for the maintenance of metazoan-specific microsyntenic gene blocks over 700 Myr of evolution.
source: Finally, we find strong evidence for cis-regulatory elements being important for the maintenance of metazoan-specific microsyntenic gene blocks over 700 Myr of evolution.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about microsynteny and enhancers.

claim: The emergence of distal enhancer regulation prior to metazoan cladogenesis could explain the pervasiveness of conserved syntenic regulatory blocks in animal genomes and the absence of these blocks in their unicellular relatives.
source: The emergence of distal enhancer regulation prior to metazoan cladogenesis could explain the pervasiveness of conserved syntenic regulatory blocks in animal genomes and the absence of these blocks in their unicellular relatives (Srivastava et al., 2010; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016; Irimia et al., 2013, 2012; Bulger and Groudine, 2011; Putnam et al., 2007; Duan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of enhancers, supported by citations.

claim: A conserved gene regulatory landscape similar to that of morphologically-complex eumetazoans appears to have been already in place at the dawn of animals, and thus likely to have originated at least 700 Mya.
source: In conclusion, a conserved gene regulatory landscape similar to that of morphologically-complex eumetazoans appears to have been already in place at the dawn of animals, and thus likely to have originated at least 700 Mya.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: There were fundamental changes in the cis-regulatory architecture of the genome along the metazoan stem, concomitant with the evolution of animal multicellularity, including the apparent origin of distal enhancers and promoter types for cell-type-specificity and developmental regulation.
source: Specifically, there appears to have been fundamental changes in the cis-regulatory architecture of the genome along the metazoan stem, concomitant with the evolution of animal multicellularity, including the apparent origin of distal enhancers and promoter types for cell-type-specificity and developmental regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Quantitative rather than qualitative differences in regulatory mechanisms likely drive the evolution and diversification of eumetazoan body plans.
source: With this in mind, we propose an evolutionary scenario in which quantitative rather than qualitative differences in regulatory mechanisms likely drive the evolution and diversification of eumetazoan body plans (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary scenario.
